answer: An inlet admits few ships, so anchorage must be rationed. Each identity needs two holders outside its own harbor to countersign its mooring, and one countersignature backs one identity, so n aliases need n distinct witnesses instead of a single ring. Every mooring is recorded with a quill that keeps the writer's name, and the k-th mooring an operator files costs k squared in bond, so a farm pays near n cubed. A lantern audit re-asks a random witness each epoch; an unconfirmed mooring voids the whole inlet and its bonds cannot be pooled or resold.
